response.answer: The David Hockney: Portraits in Print exhibition is on display at the National Gallery of Australia from September 5, 2026 to May 9, 2027. The exhibition highlights Hockney's early works and his experiences as a gay man finding his identity. The NGA holds one of the most significant collections of Hockney's works in the Southern Hemisphere.

The David Hockney: Portraits in Print exhibition will be on display at the National Gallery of Australia from September 5, 2026 to May 9, 2027.(ABC News: Matt Roberts) [...] Early works of Hockney's, such as We Two Boys Together Clinging and Two Men in a Shower, celebrated gay relationships when homosexuality was still illegal in Britain, and while those are not featured in this exhibition, his experiences are tracked through sketches as a gay man finding his identity in his early career.

Hockney piece in the exhibition. 

Hockney's A Rake's Progress, a semi-autobiographical series of 16 etchings.(ABC News: Matt Roberts) [...] Portrait of an Artist (Pool with Two Figures), painted by David Hockney (not featured in the NGA exhibition) sold for more than $124 million at auction in 2018. (Supplied: Christie's/David Hockney)

The exhibition underscores Hockney's pivotal collaboration with master printmaker Tyler.

The NGA holds more than 1,000 Hockney works, in what it describes as one of the most significant collections of Hockney in the Southern Hemisphere.

Exhibition posters and unsigned works form a separate category within the Hockney print market. While they do not carry the same long-term resale potential as numbered editions, original period posters can provide an accessible entry point for new collectors.

Buyers should distinguish clearly between original exhibition posters and later reproductions, and verify condition carefully before purchase.

Overlooked in that canon is a stranger, more private painting: _Beverly Hills Housewife_, a 12-foot portrait that Hockney painted between 1966 and ’67. A new book by critic and curator James Cahill, out in the U.K. now and in the U.S. on November 3, argues the painting captures the artist’s new, “crystalline realist” style, and ultimately reveals two people—the artist and the subject—caught in a moment of transformation.
